title: Curvature of a curve
tagline: How sharply a path bends: the turn per metre, and the circle that fits
summary: Walk along a bend in a path, and your direction of travel turns. The curvature of the path is how many degrees you turn for each metre along it. A sharper bend turns you more per metre, whether you walk fast or slow. At each place where a smooth path bends, one circle matches the bend best, and the smaller that circle, the sharper the bend.

Compute the sideways acceleration on a bend from speed and curvature.
Prove that constant curvature forces a circle in the plane but not in space.

ways_in.title: Count the turn per metre
ways_in.question: How can you measure how sharp a bend in a path is?
ways_in.explanation:
Picture a smooth, winding path across a flat park. Walk along it, and notice which way you are heading, your direction of travel. On a straight stretch, your direction of travel stays the same the whole time. On a bend, your direction of travel turns a little with every step.

How sharp is a bend? Lay a cardboard arrow on the ground, pointing ahead of you along the path. Walk 10 metres along the path, and lay a second arrow there, again pointing ahead of you along the path. Now carry the second arrow back and lay it beside the first. Keep it pointing the same way the whole time, as when you slide a ruler across a table without twisting it. Measure the angle between the two arrows. If the path bends to one side and turns you at most half a turn, 180 degrees, that angle is how far your direction of travel turned over those 10 metres. Otherwise, the arrows can show less than the whole turn.

Now divide that angle by the 10 metres. A bend that turns you 20 degrees over 10 metres turns you 2 degrees per metre. A sharper bend turns you more per metre. The turn per metre is called the curvature of the path.

A bend may sharpen or ease along the way, or switch from one side to the other. Then measure over a shorter stretch, such as 1 metre or less, to find the curvature at one place. This works on smooth paths. At a sharp corner, the whole turn happens in one step. So the shorter the stretch, the bigger the answer, and no single turn per metre fits.

Why per metre, and not per second? Walk the same bend twice as fast. You turn the same 20 degrees over the same 10 metres, only in half the time. So the curvature belongs to the path, not to your speed. Walk the bend the other way, and a turn toward your left becomes a turn toward your right, but the turn per metre is the same.

A standard 400-metre running track has two straight stretches and two bends, and each bend is half a circle. You start a bend heading one way and finish it heading the opposite way, so the bend turns you half a turn, 180 degrees. Measured where a runner in the inside lane runs, each bend is about 116 metres long, and each straight stretch about 84 metres. So the runner turns 180 divided by 116, about 1.6 degrees per metre.
ways_in.takeaway: Curvature is how many degrees your direction of travel turns per metre along a smooth path; it belongs to the path, not to your speed.

ways_in.title: The circle that fits a bend
ways_in.question: Which circle matches a bend at one place, and what does its size tell you?
ways_in.recap: The curvature of a path is how many degrees your direction of travel turns for each metre you move along it. Walk once around a circular path on flat ground. You turn steadily to one side, and you end up heading the way you started. So one lap turns you one full turn, 360 degrees.
ways_in.explanation:
Walk around a circle painted on a flat playground. Every part of a circle is alike, so the circle turns you by the same amount for every metre, all the way around.

The distance around a circle is about 6.28 times its radius, the distance from its centre to its edge. One lap turns you 360 degrees, shared out equally over that distance. So a circle of radius 10 metres, which is 62.8 metres around, turns you 360 divided by 62.8, about 5.7 degrees per metre. A circle of radius 20 metres is twice as far around, so it turns you half as much per metre.

Now pick one place where a smooth path bends. Close to that place, one circle matches the bend better than any other. That circle lies on the inner side of the bend, the side the path turns toward. Its edge passes through that place, running the same way as the path, and it turns you just as sharply as the path does. A smaller circle would turn you too sharply, and a bigger one too gently. This best-matching circle is called the osculating circle, from a Latin word for kissing.

The radius of the osculating circle is called the radius of curvature at that place. A sharp bend has a small radius of curvature, and a gentle bend a large one. On a straight stretch no circle matches, because every circle turns you. No circle matches at the exact middle of an S either, where the path switches from bending one way to bending the other.

A quick rule links the curvature and the radius of curvature. On a circle, the turn per metre is 360 degrees divided by the distance around, which is 6.28 times the radius. Because 360 divided by 6.28 is about 57, that is the same as 57 divided by the radius. The osculating circle turns you just as sharply as the bend. So at each place on a bend, the curvature in degrees per metre is about 57 divided by the radius of curvature in metres.

Suppose a gentle motorway bend has a radius of curvature of 1,000 metres. Its curvature is 57 divided by 1,000, about 0.057 degrees per metre. So a car on it turns 1 degree for about every 17 metres it travels. That is why such a bend can look almost straight from the driver's seat.
ways_in.try_it: Draw a smooth S across a sheet of paper, with one tight bend and one gentle bend. Collect round things of different sizes, such as a coin, a jar lid and a plate. At each bend, lay them on the paper in turn, with the edge touching the line from the inner side of the bend. At the tight bend, a small one follows the line best. At the gentle bend, a bigger one does. Near the middle of the S, where the bend switches sides, none of them follows the line.
ways_in.takeaway: At each place on a bend, one circle matches it best; the smaller that circle, the sharper the bend.

ways_in.title: Lengths along a wire hide its bend
ways_in.question: Could a tiny creature living on a bent wire find out that the wire is bent?
ways_in.explanation:
Imagine a tiny ant that lives on a thin wire. It can only crawl along the wire, forward or back. It carries a tiny ruler for measuring lengths along the wire.

Start with a straight wire 1 metre long, and let the ant paint a mark on it every centimetre. Then, while the ant rests, bend the wire into a wavy S shape, without stretching or squashing it anywhere.

Can the ant find out that the wire is now bent? Nothing stretched, so each mark is 1 centimetre from the next, measured along the wire, as before. Between any two places on the wire, no length along it changed. So every measurement gives the same number as before the bending, and measuring with its ruler, the ant cannot tell the S from a straight wire.

Bending a wire changes only how it lies in the space around it. You can see the bend because you look at the wire from that space. Lengths measured along the wire cannot show the bend.

If you join the ends into a ring, the ant learns that crawling 1 metre brings it back to its start. But a circular ring and an oval ring of the same length give it the same lengths, so it cannot tell how the ring bends. A fast ant would feel pushed to one side on each bend, as you do in a car. That push is not a length along the wire. It comes from the ant's motion through the space around the wire.
ways_in.try_it: Lay a piece of string that does not stretch beside a ruler, and mark the string every 2 centimetres. Lay the string along a wavy line drawn on paper, then pull it straight beside the ruler again. The marks are 2 centimetres apart, as before. Nothing about the marks tells you which parts of the string lay on a bend.
ways_in.takeaway: Lengths measured along a wire cannot show how it bends; the bend shows only from the space around the wire.

ways_in.title: Turning rate as a derivative
ways_in.question: How is curvature defined and computed for a curve given by a formula?
ways_in.explanation:
The walker in "Count the turn per metre" divided a turn by a distance walked, and a derivative makes that measurement exact. Describe a curve by its position $\mathbf r(s)$, where $s$ is the length measured along the curve. A step $ds$ along the curve has length $|d\mathbf r| = ds$, so $\hat{\mathbf T} = d\mathbf r/ds$ is a unit vector along the direction of travel. The curvature is how fast it turns:

$$\kappa = \left|\frac{d\hat{\mathbf T}}{ds}\right|, \qquad R = \frac{1}{\kappa},$$

with $R$ the radius of curvature and $\kappa$ in radians per metre. One radian is $57.3^\circ$, the 57 of "The circle that fits a bend". Differentiating $\hat{\mathbf T}\cdot\hat{\mathbf T} = 1$ gives $\hat{\mathbf T}\cdot d\hat{\mathbf T}/ds = 0$. So where $\kappa \neq 0$, $d\hat{\mathbf T}/ds = \kappa\hat{\mathbf N}$, with $\hat{\mathbf N}$ the unit normal toward the side the curve turns.

For a curve in the $xy$ plane, write $\hat{\mathbf T} = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$, with $\theta$ measured counterclockwise from the $x$ axis as seen from the $+z$ side. Then $d\hat{\mathbf T}/ds = (d\theta/ds)(-\sin\theta, \cos\theta)$, so $\kappa = |d\theta/ds|$. The signed curvature $k = d\theta/ds$ is positive when the path turns toward the walker's left, with the walker's head along $+z$, as in the course orientation convention. Walking the same curve the other way flips the sign of $k$ but not $\kappa$.

On a circle of radius $a$ walked counterclockwise, $\mathbf r = a(\cos(s/a), \sin(s/a))$, so $\theta = s/a + \pi/2$ and $k = 1/a$. Also $d\hat{\mathbf T}/ds = -\mathbf r/a^2$, which points at the centre. At any point of any curve with $\kappa \neq 0$, the osculating circle has centre $\mathbf r + R\hat{\mathbf N}$ and radius $R$; it shares the curve's position, direction and curvature there.

Curves rarely come parametrized by $s$, but $ds = |d\mathbf r|$ converts any parameter. For a graph $y(x)$ walked toward increasing $x$, the derivation "Curvature of a graph" gives $k = y''/(1+y'^2)^{3/2}$, which reduces to $y''$ where the graph is level. For a curve in space with any parameter $\lambda$ and dots for $d/d\lambda$, $\kappa = |\dot{\mathbf r}\times\ddot{\mathbf r}|/|\dot{\mathbf r}|^3$, taken here on trust.
ways_in.takeaway: Curvature is the rate at which the unit tangent turns per unit length along the curve; its reciprocal is the radius of the osculating circle.

ways_in.title: What an accelerometer reads on a bend
ways_in.question: What acceleration does moving along a curve at a given speed require?
ways_in.explanation:
The osculating circle of "Turning rate as a derivative" also sets the push you feel on a bend. A car moves along a curve with speed $v = ds/dt$, as its speedometer measures relative to the road. Its velocity is $\mathbf v = v\hat{\mathbf T}$, and the derivation "Acceleration along a curve" differentiates it:

$$\mathbf a = \frac{dv}{dt}\,\hat{\mathbf T} + v^2\kappa\,\hat{\mathbf N}.$$

The first term changes the speed. The second changes only the direction, and it points toward the centre of the osculating circle. At steady speed only the second remains, with size $v^2\kappa = v^2/R$. This is the circular-motion result, now valid at each point of any smooth path. A mass $m$ therefore needs a sideways force $mv^2\kappa$; for unit mass at unit speed that force equals $\kappa$, a mechanical definition of curvature.

An accelerometer carried in the car measures this. On a level road gravity acts vertically, so the horizontal reading is the acceleration relative to the road. At $25$ m/s, which is 90 km/h, on a bend with $R = 250$ m, the accelerometer's horizontal reading is $2.5\ \text{m/s}^2$ toward the centre, about a quarter of $g$. Doubling the speed on the same bend quadruples the reading, one reason sharp bends carry low speed limits.

Newton applied the same relation to the Moon, whose nearly circular path around Earth needs a sideways acceleration $v^2\kappa$ that gravity supplies. The observation "The Moon's sideways acceleration" gives the numbers.
ways_in.takeaway: Moving at speed v along a path, you accelerate sideways by v squared times the curvature, toward the centre of the osculating circle.

ways_in.title: What curvature determines, and where it lives
ways_in.question: What does curvature determine about a curve, and is it a property of the curve itself?
ways_in.explanation:
The signed curvature $k = d\theta/ds$ of "Turning rate as a derivative" is a complete invariant of plane curves. *Fundamental theorem of plane curves:* for continuous $k: I \to \mathbb R$ there is a unit-speed $C^2$ curve $\gamma: I \to \mathbb R^2$ with signed curvature $k$, namely $\theta(s) = \theta_0 + \int_{s_0}^{s} k$ and $\gamma(s) = \gamma_0 + \int_{s_0}^{s} (\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$, and any two such curves differ by an orientation-preserving rigid motion. Sketch: two solutions have $\theta_1 - \theta_2$ constant, a rotation, after which $\gamma_1 - \gamma_2$ is constant, a translation. In $\mathbb R^3$, curvature $\kappa > 0$ together with torsion determines a $C^3$ curve up to an orientation-preserving rigid motion; $\kappa$ alone does not.

Curvature is not intrinsic to the curve, which is what the ant in "Lengths along a wire hide its bend" found. Through arc length, every connected one-dimensional Riemannian manifold is isometric to an interval or a circle, so it has no local metric invariants; $\kappa$ records how the curve sits in the ambient space. In a Riemannian manifold $(M, g)$, a unit-speed curve has $\kappa = |\nabla_{\hat T}\hat T|$, which vanishes exactly on geodesics. For a curve on a surface in $\mathbb R^3$, $d\hat{\mathbf T}/ds$ splits into geodesic and normal parts with $\kappa^2 = \kappa_g^2 + \kappa_n^2$. For a timelike worldline with $G = c = 1$, $\nabla_u u$ is the four-acceleration, whose magnitude is the proper acceleration an accelerometer reads.

Limits: $\kappa$ needs $\gamma' \neq 0$ and two derivatives; $\hat{\mathbf N}$ is undefined where $\kappa = 0$, and a corner has a turning angle but no finite curvature; its turn acts as curvature concentrated at one point.
ways_in.takeaway: Signed curvature fixes a plane curve up to rigid motion, yet a curve has no intrinsic curvature: its curvature describes how it sits in its surrounding space.

glossary.plain_definition: How sharply a path bends at a place: the degrees your direction of travel turns per metre along it.

key_equations.name: Curvature and radius of curvature
key_equations.meaning: How fast the unit direction of travel turns per unit length; its reciprocal is the radius of curvature.
key_equations.conditions: Twice-differentiable curve with nonzero velocity; $R$ has no finite value where $\kappa = 0$.
key_equations.say_aloud: Kappa is how fast the unit tangent turns per unit arc length, and R is one over kappa.

key_equations.name: Curvature of a graph
key_equations.meaning: Signed curvature of a graph, positive where it turns toward the left of a walker heading toward increasing $x$.
key_equations.conditions: Twice-differentiable graph walked toward increasing $x$, viewed with $x$ to $y$ counterclockwise.
key_equations.say_aloud: k is y double prime over one plus y prime squared, to the three halves.

key_equations.name: Acceleration along a curve
key_equations.meaning: A change of speed along the path plus a sideways part toward the centre of the osculating circle.
key_equations.conditions: Newtonian motion with $v > 0$ relative to the frame in which the curve is drawn.
key_equations.say_aloud: a equals d v by d t along the tangent, plus v squared kappa along the normal.

derivations.title: Curvature of a graph
derivations.goal: Show that a graph $y(x)$ walked toward increasing $x$ has signed curvature $k = y''/(1+y'^2)^{3/2}$.
steps: The direction of travel makes an angle $\theta$ with the $x$ axis, with $\tan\theta = y'$ and $-\pi/2 < \theta < \pi/2$.
Differentiate with respect to $x$: $\sec^2\theta\;d\theta/dx = y''$. Since $\sec^2\theta = 1 + y'^2$, $d\theta/dx = y''/(1+y'^2)$.
Arc length obeys $ds^2 = dx^2 + dy^2$, so $ds/dx = \sqrt{1+y'^2}$.
The chain rule gives $k = d\theta/ds = (d\theta/dx)/(ds/dx) = y''/(1+y'^2)^{3/2}$.

derivations.title: Acceleration along a curve
derivations.goal: Show that a body moving along a curve with speed $v(t) > 0$ has $\mathbf a = (dv/dt)\hat{\mathbf T} + v^2\kappa\hat{\mathbf N}$.
steps: The chain rule gives $\mathbf v = d\mathbf r/dt = (d\mathbf r/ds)(ds/dt) = v\hat{\mathbf T}$.
The product rule gives $\mathbf a = (dv/dt)\hat{\mathbf T} + v\,d\hat{\mathbf T}/dt$.
The chain rule again gives $d\hat{\mathbf T}/dt = (ds/dt)\,d\hat{\mathbf T}/ds = v\kappa\hat{\mathbf N}$.
Substitute: $\mathbf a = (dv/dt)\hat{\mathbf T} + v^2\kappa\hat{\mathbf N}$, two perpendicular terms.
derivations.result: The sideways part of the acceleration has size $v^2\kappa = v^2/R$ and points toward the centre of the osculating circle.

problems.statement: Eight identical curved pieces of toy train track, each 20 centimetres long measured along the track, join to make a full circle. (a) By how many degrees does the train's direction of travel turn per centimetre? (b) The distance around a circle is about 6.28 times its radius. What is this circle's radius, which is the track's radius of curvature?
hints: A full circle is one full turn, shared by the eight pieces.

numeric.quantity: turn over one centimetre of track

solution: Around the full circle the train turns one full turn, 360 degrees. The eight pieces are alike, so each turns it 360 divided by 8, which is 45 degrees.
Each piece is 20 centimetres long, so the turn per centimetre is 45 divided by 20, which is 2.25 degrees.
The circle is 8 times 20, which is 160 centimetres around, so its radius is 160 divided by 6.28, about 25.5 centimetres.

problems.statement: (a) Show that a unit-speed plane curve with constant signed curvature $k \neq 0$ is an arc of a circle of radius $1/|k|$. (b) Show that the helix $\mathbf r(t) = (a\cos t, a\sin t, bt)$ with $a > 0$ and $b \neq 0$ has constant curvature $a/(a^2+b^2)$, so constant curvature does not force a circle in space.
problems.statement_spoken: Show that constant nonzero signed curvature makes a unit-speed plane curve an arc of a circle, and that a helix has constant curvature without being a circle.
hints: For the helix use $\kappa = |\dot{\mathbf r}\times\ddot{\mathbf r}|/|\dot{\mathbf r}|^3$.
problems.answer: (a) $\theta = \theta_0 + ks$ gives $\gamma(s) = \mathbf c + k^{-1}(\sin\theta, -\cos\theta)$, at distance $1/|k|$ from $\mathbf c$. (b) $\kappa = a\sqrt{a^2+b^2}/(a^2+b^2)^{3/2} = a/(a^2+b^2)$, and the helix lies in no plane.
key_points: A constant turning rate integrates to a circle of radius one over the size of k
The helix has constant curvature a over a squared plus b squared but lies in no plane
solution: Unit speed gives $\gamma' = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$ with $\theta' = k$, so $\theta = \theta_0 + ks$.
Integrating, $\gamma = \mathbf c + k^{-1}(\sin\theta, -\cos\theta)$ for a constant $\mathbf c$, so $|\gamma - \mathbf c| = 1/|k|$.
For the helix, $\dot{\mathbf r} = (-a\sin t, a\cos t, b)$, $\ddot{\mathbf r} = (-a\cos t, -a\sin t, 0)$ and $\dot{\mathbf r}\times\ddot{\mathbf r} = (ab\sin t, -ab\cos t, a^2)$.

So $\kappa = a\sqrt{a^2+b^2}/(a^2+b^2)^{3/2} = a/(a^2+b^2)$. A non-vertical plane would bound $z = bt$, and a vertical one would make the circular shadow on the $xy$ plane a line, so no plane contains the helix.

observations.phenomenon: The Moon's sideways acceleration around Earth
observations.connection: The Moon's nearly circular path has curvature about one over its distance, so its sideways acceleration is $v^2\kappa$. Newton compared it with falling bodies at Earth's surface, about 60 times closer to Earth's centre, where an inverse-square pull is $60^2$ times stronger.
observations.numbers: $r = 3.844\times10^{5}$ km and a sidereal month of 27.32 days give $v^2/r = 2.72\times10^{-3}\ \text{m/s}^2$, while $g/60.3^2 = 2.70\times10^{-3}\ \text{m/s}^2$, within 1 percent. The Moon's own mass accounts for that gap. Earth also falls toward the Moon, so the Moon's orbit relative to Earth's centre is set by $G(M_\oplus + M_{\rm Moon})/r^2 = 2.73\times10^{-3}\ \text{m/s}^2$, within 0.3 percent of $v^2/r$. Most of that last 0.3 percent comes from the Sun's pull on the Moon and Earth.

misconceptions.belief: A creature on a bent wire could measure that it is bent.
misconceptions.why_tempting: The bend is plain to see from outside.
misconceptions.correction: Bending without stretching changes no length along the wire, and lengths are all such a creature can measure.

misconceptions.belief: The curvature of a graph is its second derivative.
misconceptions.why_tempting: The two agree where the graph is level.
misconceptions.correction: Where the graph slopes, the second derivative must be divided by one plus the slope squared, to the three halves.

misconceptions.belief: A car rounding a bend at steady speed is not accelerating.
misconceptions.why_tempting: The speedometer reading does not change.
misconceptions.correction: The velocity changes direction, so the car accelerates toward the centre of the bend by speed squared times curvature.

checks.question: On flat ground, a circular path around a pond is 60 metres long, and a circular path around a lake is 300 metres long. You walk once around each path. By how many degrees does your direction of travel turn per metre on each? Which path bends more sharply?
checks.answer: On each path you turn steadily to one side and end up heading the way you started, so each lap turns you one full turn, 360 degrees. Every part of a circular path is alike, so that turn is shared equally among its metres. The pond path turns you 360 divided by 60, which is 6 degrees per metre. The lake path turns you 360 divided by 300, which is 1.2 degrees per metre. So the pond path bends 5 times as sharply, although both laps give the same full turn.
key_points: A lap is a full turn
The pond path bends more sharply

numeric.quantity: turn over one metre of the pond path
turn over one metre of the lake path

hints: How far do you turn in one whole lap?

checks.question: A tiny ant on a straight wire 1 metre long can only crawl along it and measure lengths along it. While the ant rests, you bend the wire into a wavy S without stretching it. Can the ant find out, by measuring lengths, that the wire is bent? Why?
checks.answer: No. Bending the wire without stretching leaves every piece of it the same length. So every length the ant measures along the wire is the same as before the bending. Those lengths are the only measurements the ant can make, so they cannot show the bend. The bend shows only from the space around the wire, where you are.
key_points: Bending without stretching keeps every length
The bend shows only from outside the wire
hints: Does bending change any length along the wire?

checks.question: For the parabola $y = x^2$, with $x$ and $y$ pure numbers, a student says the curvature at $x = 1$ is $y'' = 2$, so the radius of curvature there is $0.5$. Evaluate the claim and find the correct values.
checks.question_spoken: For y equals x squared, a student says the curvature at x equals one is the second derivative, two. Evaluate this and give the correct values.
checks.answer: The claim uses $\kappa = |y''|$, which holds where the graph is level, but not here. At $x = 1$, $y' = 2$ and $y'' = 2$, so $\kappa = 2/(1+4)^{3/2} = 2/11.18 = 0.179$ and $R = 5.59$. Only at the vertex $x = 0$, where $y' = 0$, are $\kappa = 2$ and $R = 0.5$.
key_points: Slope 2 at x equals one, so curvature is not y double prime

checks.question: A car's speedometer reads a steady 72 km/h on a level bend whose radius of curvature is 80 m. A passenger says the car is not accelerating, since its speed is constant. Evaluate the claim, and find the car's acceleration relative to the road.
checks.answer: The claim is wrong. With $dv/dt = 0$ the acceleration is $v^2\kappa\,\hat{\mathbf N}$, because the direction of the velocity changes. With $v = 72$ km/h $= 20$ m/s and $\kappa = 1/(80\ \text{m})$, $a = (20\ \text{m/s})^2/(80\ \text{m}) = 5.0\ \text{m/s}^2$, about half of $g$, toward the centre of the osculating circle.
key_points: 5.0 metres per second squared toward the centre
hints: Convert 72 km/h to metres per second.

novice.retell_attempt:
When you walk around a bend, the way you face turns. Curvature is how many degrees you turn for every metre, so 20 degrees in 10 metres is 2 per metre, and walking faster doesn't change it. A running-track bend turns you 180 degrees in 116 metres, about 1.6 a metre, though I thought each bend was 100 metres. Circles turn you the same all the way round, and a smaller circle turns you more per metre. At any spot on a bend some circle fits best, called the osculating circle, and its radius is the radius of curvature; I didn't follow where the 57 came from or how it gives 17 metres. I wasn't sure how to carry the stick back along a curvy path without it swinging. An ant on a wire can't tell the wire got bent, because bending doesn't change any length along it; only we can see the bend from outside. But it could feel pushed if it ran fast, so maybe it could tell after all?

Second novice pass, reading revision 5 before any fix: Curvature is how much your direction of travel turns for every metre you walk, so 20 degrees over 10 metres is 2 degrees per metre, and it is the same whether you run or stroll. I laid one stick pointing ahead, walked 10 metres, laid another, and carried the second back without twisting it, but with both lying on the grass I could not see which end of each was the front, and on the running-track bend they came back along the same line, so I did not know whether to write 0 or 180. I also stopped at 'you turn a whole angle within a single step' and wondered which angle that was. A circle turns you 360 degrees over its whole way round, so a small circle turns you more per metre than a big one; at any spot on a bend the circle that fits best is the osculating circle and its radius is the radius of curvature. There is a rule that curvature is about 57 divided by that radius, but the sentence that introduces it says it links 'the two numbers' and I had to look back to see which two. An ant on a wire cannot find out by measuring that the wire was bent, because bending changes no length along it; only we, looking from the space around the wire, can see the bend.
